article_title: Everyday Mathematics®
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Balance teacher-directed instruction with open-ended problem solving, hands-on exploration, and varied skills practice in mathematics lessons
description: Everyday Mathematics® embodies balanced instruction: "Each lesson includes whole-class instruction and small-group, partner, or individual activities. This structure balances teacher-directed instruction with open-ended problem solving, hands-on explorations, long-term projects, and ongoing practice." Basic skills practice is provided through multiple methods, including "written and oral fact practice, fluency activities and tests, mental math activities, daily sets of review problems, homework assignments, and a variety of math games."
requirements: Lesson structures that pair whole-class teacher-led segments with small-group, partner, or individual activities, plus recurring practice opportunities across multiple formats
target_learning_goals: mathematics concepts, skills fluency, and real-life problem solving
examples: In the reviewed implementation, daily lesson plans usually began with a Math Message as the focus of the lesson, combining teacher-led discussions and hands-on group and individual activities, with student journals and homework reinforcing practical experience.
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/166

article_title: Building Assets Reducing Risks (BARR) — Attendance
citation: Building Assets Reducing Risks (BARR) program evidence summary. (2020). https://www.barrcenter.org
title: Sustain model implementation with multi-year sequenced professional development plus ongoing dedicated coaching
description: BARR pairs annual in-person training with continuous coaching: each school receives "two days of in-person professional development annually delivered through a sequenced, multi-year training plan," and "an average of more than 200 hours per year of personalized coaching and technical assistance." Year 1 training focuses on implementing the model; Years 2 and 3 address advanced topics such as effective team meetings, understanding trauma, reducing risky behaviors, and fostering student resilience.
requirements: A dedicated BARR coach assigned to each school providing structured weekly coaching sessions and quarterly on-site visits.
A sequenced, multi-year training plan using BARR materials and practice.
target_learners: teachers and school leaders implementing BARR
target_learning_goals: faithful implementation of the BARR model
continuous improvement and long-term sustainability
examples: BARR coordinators and administrators also join quarterly Professional Learning Community calls and attend the annual BARR National Conference.

article_title: Beyond "Treatment versus Control": How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research
citation: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2018). Beyond "Treatment versus Control": How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Working Paper 61. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use Bayesian methods to make factorial experiments with many treatment arms feasible in education research
description: The paper recommends that researchers interested in studying complex interventions adopt Bayesian analysis for factorial designs. Because traditional inference "may require prohibitively large sample sizes to perform complex factorial experiments," Bayesian methods with hierarchical priors and partial pooling make "factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible," enabling testing of multiple implementation factors such as dosages and implementation strategies and their interactions.
requirements: A research question involving a large set of related interventions or implementation factors suited to a factorial design
constraints: The feasibility advantage is demonstrated for complex experiments with many factors and factor levels
target_learning_goals: Designing efficient experiments that test multiple factors and interactions
examples: Power calculations for a U.S. Department of Education experiment showed Bayesian designs reaching a given MDE with roughly half the sample size needed classically for 72 treatment arms
key_sources: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2018). Beyond "Treatment versus Control": How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Working Paper 61. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/beyond-treatment-versus-control-how-bayesian-analysis-makes-factorial-experiments-feasible

article_title: Understanding Types of Evidence: A Guide for Educators
citation: Gregory Chojnacki, Alexandra Resch, Alma Vigil, Ignacio Martinez, Steve Bates. (2016). Understanding Types of Evidence: A Guide for Educators. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: When choosing technologies, base decisions on evidence about which options are effective
description: The guide recommends that educators making technology decisions ground their choices in effectiveness evidence rather than in marketing claims alone. It states: "When making decisions about which technologies to use, you need evidence about which options are effective to make the best possible use of your technology budget." The guide then equips educators to judge evidence quality by describing its four evidence types.
requirements: Access to information sources containing evidence about the effectiveness of the technology options under consideration
constraints: Framed for decisions about which technologies to use and how to allocate a technology budget
target_learning_goals: making evidence-informed technology purchasing decisions
examples: The guide orders its four evidence types from weakest to strongest and pairs each with examples of information sources, so readers can locate stronger evidence for effectiveness claims

article_title: Challenges and Solutions in Evaluation Technical Assistance During Design and Early Implementation
citation: Andrew Gothro, Elías S. Hanno, M. C. Bradley. (2022). Challenges and Solutions in Evaluation Technical Assistance During Design and Early Implementation. title: Balance program or initiative requirements with evaluation needs when providing evaluation technical assistance
description: The article identifies balancing "program or initiative requirements and evaluation needs" as a central challenge in providing evaluation technical assistance during design and early implementation. Because grantees are developing interventions and planning or conducting evaluations at the same time, ETA providers must attend to both the funder's requirements and the evaluation's methodological needs. The article concludes with thoughts on how to make ETA successful in this balancing act.
requirements: ETA providers and liaisons engaged with grantees during both intervention design and evaluation planning
constraints: The challenge arises during design and early implementation of grant-funded interventions
target_learning_goals: Conducting evaluations that satisfy initiative requirements while producing useful evidence
examples: The case study devotes a section to balancing program or initiative requirements and evaluation needs across the YARH and P3 initiatives.

article_title: An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations. Education Review, vol. 33, no. 6.
title: Address the multiple testing problem in impact evaluations using a framework that balances Type I and Type II errors
description: When an evaluation tests many outcomes and subgroups, the article recommends addressing the resulting multiple testing problem with a framework that "balances Types I and II errors". This directs evaluators to choose testing procedures that jointly manage the risk of spurious impact findings and the risk of missing true effects, rather than focusing on only one error type.
requirements: An evaluation design involving hypothesis tests across multiple outcomes and/or subgroups
target_learners: Education and social policy researchers conducting impact evaluations
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of impact findings across multiple tested outcomes and subgroups
examples: The article discusses this balancing framework as its proposed approach for social policy impact evaluations.

article_title: Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues
citation: May, Henry, Irma Perez-Johnson, Joshua Haimson, Samina Sattar, and Phil Gleason (2009). Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues (NCEE 2009-013). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Collect and use baseline state test data as covariates to increase statistical power and reduce study costs
description: The paper recommends that studies using student achievement outcomes generally aim to collect and use baseline data, because analyses using more than one wave of data typically have much greater statistical power than posttest-only analyses. Using prior state test results as baseline covariates can substantially reduce overall study costs, since the power improvement allows the sample size to be greatly reduced while maintaining the target power level. Baseline data also help establish treatment-control equivalence and assess potential nonresponse bias.
requirements: Researchers must link pretest and posttest scores for individual students under student-level random assignment, or link individual and/or aggregate data under school- or district-level random assignment
constraints: Substantial effort may be required to link longitudinal data; costs of linking must be evaluated separately for each state because database quality varies
target_learning_goals: Increased statistical power for detecting intervention impacts on student achievement
examples: The paper cites Bloom, Richburg-Hayes, and Black (2005) showing that even aggregate school-level baseline covariates can dramatically increase the power of a school-level RCT
key_sources: May, Henry, Irma Perez-Johnson, Joshua Haimson, Samina Sattar, and Phil Gleason (2009). Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues (NCEE 2009-013). article_title: Navigating the Shift to Intensive Principal Preparation in Illinois
citation: McIlhagga, Doug. (2016). Study Finds Successes, Challenges in Illinois Shift to Intensive Principal Preparation. Illinois Education Research Council at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. https://ierc.education
title: Balance quality and quantity when making principal preparation more selective and intensive
description: This principle, drawn from the study's lead author, holds that selective, intensive principal preparation reforms succeed only if the reduced pipeline of graduates remains sufficient to meet demand for school leaders. The study reports that preparation programs experienced substantial, but not unexpected, declines in enrollment after the shift to targeted and selective preparation, while stakeholders valued the higher quality. As Bradford R. White puts it, "Finding a balance between quality and quantity is going to be a key to the success of this policy moving forward."
requirements: Monitor whether the supply of principals prepared in more selective programs is sufficient to meet statewide demand
constraints: Enrollment declines followed the shift to selective, principal-specific preparation, per the study
target_learners: Prospective and practicing school principals in university preparation programs
target_learning_goals: School leadership capability and capacity to improve schools and raise student achievement
examples: Illinois' 2014-15 policy shift from a general administrative training model to targeted, selective principal-specific preparation across state universities

Illinois Education Research Council at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/navigating-shift-intensive-principal-preparation-illinois-depth-look-stakeholder

article_title: Assessment education: Bridging research, theory, and practice to promote equity and student learning
citation: Tarasawa, B., Gotwals, A., & Jackson, C. (2020). Assessment education: Bridging research, theory, and practice to promote equity and student learning. Rowman & Littlefield. https://rowman.com
title: Use assessment in a way that balances addressing opportunity gaps, especially under COVID-era schooling challenges
description: The book promotes using assessment not only for accountability but deliberately balanced to address opportunity gaps. Its description calls this balancing "a critical element now more than ever as schools face the challenge of education in the era of COVID." The principle frames assessment as an equity tool for educators pursuing data-informed instruction rather than purely punitive measurement.

constraints: The book presents this as especially critical in the era of COVID, when schools face heightened challenges
target_learners: K-12 students in schools addressing opportunity gaps
target_learning_goals: Equitable learning outcomes supported by data-informed instruction
examples: The book compiles resources and strategies for teachers, administrators, and educational leaders who strive toward data-informed instruction that balances assessment use to address opportunity gaps.

article_title: Assessment During Collaborative Learning
citation: Fusco, J., DiMaria, S., Yeadon, B., Kolodner, J., & Shell, A. (2025). Assessment During Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/252
title: Balancing individual and group assessment in collaborative learning with pre-, checkpoint, and follow-up individual measures
description: The primer recommends a deliberate mix of individual and group assessments so that collaborative work stays meaningful while individual learning remains visible. Some practitioners find "a mix of 40% collaborative group grades and 60% individual grades encourages students to engage seriously in collaborative work" while still showing individual abilities. Concrete moves include documenting individual thinking before collaboration, checkpoint assessments during the process, follow-up individual assessments after group activities, and assessments capturing collective learning.
requirements: Preplanning what to assess and when; individual knowledge checks follow up when collaborative assessments do not reveal what each student can do
constraints: Students and parents typically prefer individual assessment and may find grades for collaborative work confusing or disappointing
target_learners: K-12 and STEM students working in collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: Content mastery
collaborative skills
individual accountability
examples: Practitioners use pre/post individual assessments of growth or individual quizzes after group tasks when group work does not uncover what each student can do

Flexibility for educators to be responsive to student priorities and needs

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Balance routine and non-routine problems in classroom problem solving
description: The guide's final structural recommendation is that "teachers should try to strike a balance between routine and non-routine problems." Routine problems are solvable by familiar step-by-step methods and "can help students strengthen their understanding of an operation or mathematical idea." Non-routine problems lack predictable solution paths and "help students think strategically and apply mathematics in new situations." The pattern pairs the two problem types across instruction.
requirements: A supplementary supply of both routine and non-routine problems, since textbooks may not provide enough of either type.
constraints: What counts as non-routine is relative: what is non-routine for a less experienced problem solver may be routine for more advanced students.
target_learning_goals: Strengthening understanding of operations and ideas (routine) and strategic thinking and applying mathematics in new situations (non-routine)
examples: Routine problems may be cognitively demanding and multi-step yet still follow familiar methods; non-routine problems require grappling with new skills and concepts not yet mastered.

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students
citation: Nagaoka, J., & Healey, K. (2016). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2015: A focus on four-year college degrees. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. http://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/educational-attainment-chicago-public-schools-students-2015-focus-four-year-college
title: Bachelor's Degree Attainment Index and Direct Bachelor's DAI metrics
description: The UChicago Consortium developed two metrics to estimate students' progression to and through college: the Bachelor's DAI and the Direct Bachelor's DAI. The Direct Bachelor's DAI counts students taking "the straight-forward path of graduating high school in four years, enrolling immediately in a four-year college, and earning a four-year college degree within six years of starting college," estimated at 16 percent for 2015. The Bachelor's DAI additionally counts students who first enroll in a two-year college or delay entry before earning a four-year degree, yielding 18 percent.
requirements: Requires district data on high school graduation, immediate four-year college enrollment, and six-year college graduation rates, plus data on delayed-entry and two-year-entry pathways for the Bachelor's DAI
constraints: The brief notes a national Bachelor's DAI cannot be calculated because comparable data on bachelor's degree completion for students who delay college entry are not available
target_learning_goals: Progression to and through four-year college degree attainment

article_title: Foundations for Young Adult Success: A Developmental Framework
citation: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). A Framework for Developing Young Adult Success in the 21st Century: White Paper — Defining Young Adult Success. University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research Working Paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/framework-developing-young-adult-success-21st-century
title: Four-part conception of agency: intentionality, forethought, self-reactiveness, self-reflectiveness
description: The framework adopts Bandura's (2006) four-part definition of agency to explain how young adults shape their life course. Agency means "taking an active role in shaping and managing one's chosen path rather than being at the mercy of external forces" (an internal versus external locus of control). The four parts are intentionality (action plan and strategies), forethought (setting goals and anticipating outcomes), self-reactiveness (self-regulation and competence to act), and self-reflectiveness (reflecting on efficacy and adjusting course).
requirements: The framework treats agency as resting on key factors — purpose, values, mindsets, competence, and relationships — that come together in an integrated identity
target_learning_goals: goal-setting, self-regulation, self-reflection, and directing one's own life course
examples: The article derives guiding questions such as "Who am I and what do I value?" and "Do I believe I can accomplish them?" from this agency conceptualization

article_title: Strategic Resource Allocation for the 21st Century: How State Leaders Can Address the Silent Recession
citation: Krausen, K., Caparas, R., Ripma, T., & Willis, J. (2020). Strategic resource allocation for the 21st century: How state leaders can address the silent recession. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/strategic-resource-allocation/
title: State funding models should balance targeted funds for student needs with sufficient local flexibility
description: The report argues that state K–12 funding system design matters as much as funding levels: "An effective school funding model should provide targeted funds to ensure that spending aligns with state priorities and serves all students equitably, but should also allow sufficient flexibility for school districts to use funds to meet their local needs." It notes most states use foundation formulas with weighted student formulas, and that states have shifted toward local flexibility over the past decade while some archaic provisions (e.g., obsolete small-district thresholds) work against desired outcomes.
requirements: States control how education funding is structured and distributed through the design of their funding system, so the principle applies at the state policy level
constraints: The report notes evidence suggests foundation formulas tend to be the most effective at ensuring adequacy, but states must also weigh targeting versus flexibility tradeoffs
target_learners: K–12 public school students, including economically disadvantaged students, English learners, and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of resources to support state goals for student performance
examples: Most states' formulas now distribute additional funds to LEAs based on student characteristics such as low-income and English learner status; high-performing states also account for regional cost differences, district size, and school type

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Balance the technical, adaptive, and relational elements of school safety rather than emphasizing only technical implementation
description: The guide defines technical elements as policies, plans, structures, and models handed down to be implemented; adaptive elements as the mindsets, values, and belief systems needed to tailor them; and relational elements as social capital, belonging, collectivism, and trust. It warns that "Implementing school safety through only a technical lens is like sitting on a stool with two of its legs missing; all three are needed for success." Without the adaptive mindsets in place, implementation can be inconsistent and unsustainable over time.
requirements: Deep levels of community engagement and collectively shared values and beliefs are needed for the technical elements of transformational school safety to function at their best.
constraints: The guide states that tools and practices put in place for reimagined safety may be oppositional to the values, mindsets, and practices schools have been operating with systemically.
target_learning_goals: sustainable implementation of school safety initiatives
school climate and culture change
examples: The guide's practice exercise has participants draw three concentric circles to map a technical element, the people it affects, and the beliefs that led to its creation.

citation: Amin Jalali. (2026). AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06207

citation: Rose Niousha, Samantha Boatright Smith, Bita Akram, Peter Brusilovsky, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, John DeNero, and Narges Norouzi. (2026). The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05648

MisconceptionTutor "extends the baseline tutor with two additional structured steps": identifying likely student misconceptions from an instructor-authored list and generating feedback that explicitly targets them, output as structured JSON with only the feedback field shown to students.

article_title: The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness
citation: Rose Niousha, Samantha Boatright Smith, Bita Akram, Peter Brusilovsky, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, John DeNero, and Narges Norouzi. (2026). The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05648
title: Evaluate AI tutors jointly along pedagogical quality and student engagement dimensions
description: The article argues that pedagogical quality is a prerequisite but insufficient evaluation axis for AI tutors: once tutors reach a high pedagogical standard, rubric-based metrics differentiate systems poorly, and feedback can be pedagogically sound yet unhelpful if students do not engage with it. Evaluation frameworks should therefore "jointly consider pedagogical quality and student engagement", since optimizing for either alone risks technically sound but insufficiently engaging feedback or superficial success.
requirements: Pedagogical rubric assessment to establish a baseline bar for instructional quality
Behavioral engagement metrics grounded in logged student interaction data
constraints: Engagement metrics capture immediate uptake, not longer-term learning outcomes; high success scores can reflect answer copying rather than learning
target_learners: students in courses deploying LLM-based AI tutors
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of AI tutor effectiveness in real learning environments
examples: Applying DAMR and RelScore/SuccScore to 10,235 submissions from two semesters revealed tutor differences in engagement not captured by pedagogy-only evaluation

article_title: Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions
citation: Feng Z and Huang K (2026) Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions. Front. Psychol. 17:1879982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1879982
title: Integrated framework combining Bayesian cognitive diagnosis, knowledge space theory, and cognitive load theory for personalized path optimization
description: The article proposes and validates "a personalized learning path optimization framework that integrates Bayesian cognitive diagnosis, knowledge space theory, and cognitive load theory." Bayesian DINA estimation supplies attribute mastery probabilities on sparse data; knowledge space theory supplies prerequisite ordering so that "prerequisite attributes must be learned before target attributes"; and cognitive load theory supplies the psychological mechanism, since prerequisite-respecting sequences are held to reduce extraneous load. The framework links diagnosis, sequencing, and mediation testing in one pipeline.
requirements: A Q-matrix mapping items to cognitive attributes and a specified attribute prerequisite hierarchy
Sufficient response data for MCMC estimation of the Bayesian DINA model
constraints: The attribute hierarchy is a theory-driven specification based on Bloom's taxonomy rather than an official structure provided by EdNet
The framework was validated on foundational probability content with undergraduates and on EdNet KT1 listening/reading skill tags interpreted as general cognitive attributes
target_learners: undergraduate students learning foundational probability theory
online platform learners in large-scale educational datasets
target_learning_goals: mastery of prerequisite-ordered cognitive attributes such as foundation concepts, rule application, logical reasoning, procedural knowledge, and analytical thinking
examples: The experimental group followed personalized paths generated by the shortest remediation path algorithm while the control group followed a fixed A1→A2→A3→A4→A5 sequence over the same content.

article_title: Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery
citation: Gupta, L. R., Kaur, K., Ram, D. S., & Parani, P. (2026). Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery. arXiv preprint, under review at IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://arxiv.org
title: BAVD: a behaviourally-adaptive visual diversion model for digital assessment rendering
description: BAVD is a coupled dynamical-systems model in which a synthetic, non-semantic visual field is composited with assessment content and modulated in real time by observed candidate behaviour. The article states that the underlying question content is never altered, reworded, or restructured; only the visual presentation carries an adaptive, low-intensity diversion signal. The model comprises a Diversion Field Generator, a Rendering Tensor, a Behaviour Tensor, a Composite Integrity Functional, and a Multi-dimensional Entropy Functional, with diversion intensity treated as a first-class adaptive variable governed jointly by behavioural evidence and a candidate's declared accessibility profile.
requirements: A per-session secret key delivered to the rendering client over an authenticated channel, since the diversion field is keyed to a per-session secret and its resistance to capture rests on that key rather than on the adversary being unfamiliar with the construction.
constraints: The mechanism addresses screen-capture and screen-sharing adversaries; a compromised client that reads true content before compositing, and an adversary who memorises items, are out of scope and not addressable at the rendering layer.
The paper is a theoretical contribution and reports no platform performance data.

target_learning_goals: maintaining assessment integrity during digital assessment delivery

article_title: Guardrails or Roadblocks? Effects of Pedagogical Style and Context Awareness in AI Teaching Assistants for Programming
citation: Madeleine Eastwood, Harshith Narne, Joseph Hilby, Paul Denny, Ashish Aggarwal, and Amanpreet Kapoor. (2026). Guardrails or Roadblocks? Effects of Pedagogical Style and Context Awareness in AI Teaching Assistants for Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29995
title: Balance pedagogical guidance style and context awareness in AI TA design rather than treating more scaffolding or more context as inherently better
description: The article argues that guardrailed AI teaching assistants are effective only when their pedagogical guidance and contextual awareness fit the task and the student. It reports that "guardrails can become roadblocks when pedagogical guidance and contextual awareness are not well balanced": a Socratic chatbot with limited context demanded high effort, while a rigidly Socratic chatbot with full context was rated least favorably. Educators should configure guidance style according to whether the assignment goal is task completion, conceptual understanding, or productive struggle.

Full context alone did not ensure support felt useful or led to stronger understanding

The principle directs educators to adopt AI as a tool for scientific inquiry without displacing human agency in experimentation.

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: Bayesian formulation of BKT: priors, posterior inference, and hierarchical partial pooling
description: The article frames BKT estimation as Bayesian inference: parameters are treated as random variables with prior distributions, and inference targets the posterior P(theta | Y), which "explicitly captures parameter uncertainty" and propagates it to downstream analyses such as mastery trajectories and group comparisons. The framework motivates Bayesian estimation on four grounds: principled uncertainty quantification, incorporation of prior knowledge for regularization, mitigation of BKT identifiability issues via informative priors, and natural extension to hierarchical models with partial pooling across students, skills, or items, which is "particularly beneficial in sparse-data settings common in educational experiments."
requirements: Approximate inference (MCMC or variational) is required because exact inference is intractable due to exponentially many latent state sequences
constraints: Approximate methods such as VI and Pathfinder produce biased approximations that often underestimate posterior uncertainty and simplify dependencies among parameters
target_learners: students in intelligent tutoring systems and educational experiments modeled via knowledge tracing
target_learning_goals: quantifying uncertainty in learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters for adaptive instruction and intervention comparison
examples: StanBKT implements this formulation with logit-scale priors, half-scaled-logit bounds on guess and slip, and hierarchical priors with learned between-group variance

This processing instruction approach "involves explanation and practice/experience processing input data, taking learner strategies in input processing as the starting point," in contrast to traditional instruction's explanation plus output practice.

article_title: Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives
citation: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7
title: Social-cognitive account of observational learning: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation as subfunctions
description: The review presents Bandura's account of how modeling examples work: observers acquire a cognitive (symbolic) representation of the model's behavior that outlasts the modeling situation, so "observational learning can occur without imitation taking place". Effective observational learning requires attention to the relevant aspects of modeled behavior, retention via constructive encoding and rehearsal, ability to reproduce depending on representation quality and component skills, and motivation determining whether the behavior is exhibited. The review uses this to explain why model characteristics and attentional processes matter in modeling example design.
requirements: The learner must pay attention to the relevant aspects of the modeled behavior
constraints: Modeled behavior that is too complex for the learner may result in fragmentary learning; novices may have difficulty detecting errors and may rehearse faulty behavior
target_learning_goals: acquisition of cognitive and motor skills through observation

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Balance game features for motivation against instructional features for learning
description: The book recommends that designers manage a fundamental design tension: "Designing effective educational games always involves a tension between including game features for entertainment and instructional features for learning." Game features can promote motivation and generative processing but can also distract the learner and increase extraneous processing; instructional features can guide attention and prime deeper processing but can destroy the fun of game playing and reduce willingness to engage. The challenge is to balance the positive and negative aspects to suit the needs of each learner.
requirements: Designers must include both game features, intended to motivate engagement, and instructional features, intended to foster appropriate cognitive processing
constraints: Instructional features can diminish motivation to learn by reducing the fun of game playing; game features can diminish learning by increasing extraneous processing
target_learners: learners playing educational games in schools and training programs
target_learning_goals: deep learning outcomes through motivated, generative cognitive processing

article_title: Stealth assessment of creativity in a physics video game
citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Bayesian network evidence accumulation for real-time competency estimation in games
description: The article implements stealth assessment using Bayesian networks (BNs), one per level, with creativity as a parent node of fluency, flexibility, and originality child nodes. At the end of each level, log files are parsed, observables identified (Evidence Identification) and scored, then absorbed by the level-specific BN (Evidence Accumulation), updating probabilistic competency estimates in real time. BNs offer graphical representation, learning from data, immediate updating, and fast scoring with discrete variables, making them suited for embedded scoring engines.

Expected maximization and gradient descent algorithms to update conditional probability tables
constraints: Prior probabilities depend on expert judgments about indicator distributions

article_title: Working Memory Model and Language Learning
citation: Demir, Bora. (2021). Working Memory Model and Language Learning. Shanlax International Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.34293/education.v9iS2-Sep.4366
title: Baddeley's multi-component Working Memory model as a framework for language learning
description: The article takes Baddeley's (2012) Working Memory model as its theoretical framework for understanding language learning. WM is described as "a complex and limited cognitive system" that enables input "to be temporarily stored, monitored and manipulated". The model comprises a central executive and three slave systems — the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and the episodic buffer — each handling different information types. The article uses this structure to map specific WM components onto specific language-learning processes.

constraints: The article notes the model is "not perfectly specified" and "the components of the model and their interrelationships are underspecified" (Andrade, 2001, as cited)

The central executive "remains the least understood component of the model"

Because it can evolve as data are analyzed, it serves as a tool for learning at multiple levels.

article_title: The structure of working memory in young children and its relation to intelligence
citation: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/
title: Baddeley's multi-component working memory models: three-factor (1974) and four-factor with episodic buffer (2000)
description: Baddeley and Hitch's three-factor model includes "central executive, visuospatial sketchpad, and phonological loop factors," with the phonological loop as a temporary store for speech-based information refreshed by rehearsal and the visuospatial sketchpad as a temporary store for visual and spatial information. Baddeley's 2000 four-factor model added "an episodic buffer" described as a back-up store capable of integrating phonological, visual, and other types of information over space and time, forming an interface between the subsystems and long-term memory. The study tested both models in children; the three-factor model fit well but slightly worse than Cowan's, and the four-factor model failed because the episodic buffer was indistinguishable from the visuospatial sketchpad.
requirements: Requires indicators for each factor, including binding tasks to test the episodic buffer's proposed integrative storage functions
constraints: In this child sample the episodic buffer factor could not be empirically differentiated from the visuospatial sketchpad factor, so the four-factor model was not viable
target_learners: young school-age children aged 7-9 with typical development
target_learning_goals: understanding competing structural accounts of working memory components relevant to learning and assessment
examples: The four-factor model was tested with episodic buffer indicators comprising phonological binding, visuospatial binding, and cross-modal binding tasks

citation: Ottoboni Giovanni, Ceciliani Andrea, Tessari Alessia. (2021). The Effect of Structured Exercise on Short-Term Memory Subsystems: New Insight on Training Activities. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18147545

As the article states, it "includes the two STM subsystems specific for visuo-spatial information and auditory-verbal information postulated by Baddley and an STM subsystem specific for visuo-motor information, i.e., the gestural buffer". The study uses this structure to predict which subsystems acute open- versus closed-skill exercise should affect.

article_title: The double-edged sword of pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery
citation: Bonawitz Elizabeth, Shafto Patrick, Gweon Hyowon, Goodman Noah D., Spelke Elizabeth, Schulz Laura. (2011). The Double-edged Sword of Pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2010.10.001
title: Bayesian pedagogical-sampling model of instruction as an inductive bias
description: The article formalizes pedagogical learning as rational inference under reciprocal assumptions: a learner rationally updates beliefs given data, and a helpful teacher chooses demonstrations likely to increase the learner's belief in the correct hypothesis (Equations 1' and 2). Under pedagogical sampling, "the learner will infer, by Equation 1’, that the demonstrated functions are exhaustive—all the functions will be demonstrated by a helpful teacher." Under default (weak) sampling, evidence about tested affordances provides no information about untested ones. The model predicts the exploration trade-off tested in both experiments.
requirements: The inference depends on the learner believing the data were chosen by a knowledgeable, helpful teacher; if evidence is sampled randomly or the teacher is interrupted, the default sampling assumption applies and absence of additional functions is not inferred.
constraints: The article treats interrupted or naive demonstrations as non-pedagogical even with superficial ostensive cues; the qualitative conclusion is stated to hold under further iterations of the equations, with scope limited to the modeled pedagogical situations.
target_learning_goals: causal learning about novel objects' latent functions
calibrating exploration versus exploitation in discovery
examples: The model motivated Experiment 1's prediction that pedagogically sampled evidence would yield briefer, narrower play and fewer discovered functions, and Experiment 2's 'similar priors' prediction for overheard instruction.

article_title: The relationship between expressive vocabulary knowledge and reading skills for adult struggling readers
citation: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x

Instructors should instead remain mindful of a balanced approach combining word-reading skills, fluency activities, vocabulary development, and reading comprehension strategies.

Vocabulary development

citation: Negen, J., Sarnecka, B. W., & Lee, M. D. (2011). An Excel sheet for inferring children's number-knower levels from give-N data. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0134-4
title: The Lee and Sarnecka Bayesian knower-level model of give-N task behavior
description: A probabilistic generative model in which children's give-N answers are understood as Bayesian reasoning based on prior knowledge of number concepts and trial-by-trial experimenter instructions. It specifies a base rate — a distribution of prior probabilities describing what chance responding looks like — which is updated by an evidence value v when the child is asked for N items: known meanings become more likely, other known meanings less likely, and unknown meanings retain base-rate relative probabilities. The article implements it as a graphical model with a knower-level parameter per child.

constraints: The article states implementing the full model would require most developmental researchers to learn a host of new technical skills

target_learning_goals: inferring stages of number-word and cardinality concept development (knower levels)
examples: The article applies the model to 423 calibration sessions to obtain point probabilities for the Excel approximation, e.g. the chance that a 1-knower gives 1 when asked for one is 83.33%

article_title: Violations of Core Knowledge Shape Early Learning
citation: Stahl Aimee E., Feigenson Lisa. (2019). Violations of Core Knowledge Shape Early Learning. Topics in Cognitive Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/tops.12389
title: Bayesian prior-strength account of surprise-driven learning from core versus acquired knowledge
description: The article proposes a Bayesian framework in which learners hold priors of varying strength—innate (core knowledge) or learned—and update them to posteriors upon observing events. The larger the prior-to-posterior discrepancy, the greater the surprise and "perhaps the greater the subsequent learning." On this quantitative view, priors set by core knowledge are stronger than those set by acquired associations, so their violation produces larger updates and greater learning enhancement. The authors offer this as one framework that might capture the potency of core versus acquired knowledge violations, while stressing it remains to be tested.
requirements: Empirical approaches capable of quantifying the degree of surprise learners experience and mapping it to subsequent learning, as the authors state will be needed
constraints: The article states this quantitative characterization of core versus acquired violations remains to be seen and will require extended efforts using multiple empirical approaches
target_learning_goals: acquisition of new object properties and word labels following expectancy violation
examples: The gumball machine experiments tested whether improbable events produce graded learning, as a continuous Bayesian account would predict, and found step-like performance instead

citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7

citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7

citation: Benzi Slakmon, Rotem Abdu. (2024). Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19:137–155. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09423-6
title: Bakhtinian dialogic framework of four interconnected themes — voices, expanding the dialogue, inter-animation, and relations — as an analytical lens for collaborative dialogue
description: The article operationalizes dialogue through four Bakhtin-inspired themes used both to train teachers and to analyze noticing utterances. constraints: The article warns noticing dialogue cannot be reduced to best-practice behaviors, since attending and responding require balancing the dialogic tension between correctness and additional voices.

target_learning_goals: noticing and supporting productive student dialogue during collaborative learning
examples: The intervention lesson asked teachers to write definitions of dialogue, discussed practices such as allocating individual thinking time before group learning, and asked them to list what they would pay attention to in collaborative learning.

description: The article recommends that educational standards and policy documents draw on program-based, randomized controlled, and correlational studies together rather than privileging one category. title: Backfire effects: knowledge, attitude, and worldview backfire in refutation
description: The article defines backfire effects as "the ironic reinforcement of a misconception after an attempted refutation". Math and gender are argued to be identity-relevant domains, making worldview and attitude backfire plausible when refuting math-gender misconceptions.

citation: Flunger, B., Verdonschot, A., Zitzmann, S., Hornstra, L., & van Gog, T. (2024). A Bayesian approach to students' perceptions of teachers' autonomy support. Learning and Instruction, 91, 101873. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101873

description: The article recommends that parents align their aspirations with their realistic expectations rather than aspiring far beyond them: 'These results highlight the need for parents to balance their expectations and aspirations to support their children's emotional well-being and academic success.' constraints: Raising expectations alone is not uniformly beneficial, since higher expectations predicted higher anxiety, anger, and shame the following year
target_learning_goals: students' achievement emotions and emotional well-being in mathematics
examples: The study measured parental expectation and aspiration with single items each year and found over-aspiration predicted same-year anxiety and lower pride.

citation: R. P. (1922). Reviews of Ballard, Group Tests of Intelligence and Carothers, Psychological Examinations of College Students. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 380-381. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Ballard's definition of intelligence as relative general efficiency of minds under similar conditions
description: The reviewed book contains a simple chapter on the nature of intelligence in which various definitions are discussed and which the reviewer calls admirably written. It closes with the author's own definition, offered as a working conceptualization: intelligence is the relative general efficiency of a mind, measured only when conditions of knowledge, interest, and habituation are held similar across those compared. The book also treats correlation and statistical procedure and the use of group tests in schools in the same simple manner. As the reviewer quotes, "Intelligence is the relative general efficiency of minds measured under similar conditions of knowledge, interest and habituation."
requirements: Comparisons of intelligence must be made under similar conditions of knowledge, interest, and habituation
target_learning_goals: Understanding and measuring intelligence as measured mental efficiency
examples: The book's closing definition in its chapter on the nature of intelligence

citation: Robert Fairlie and Prashant Loyalka. (2020). Schooling and Covid-19: lessons from recent research on EdTech. npj Science of Learning 5:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00072-6
title: Balance remote learning by intermingling work on electronic devices with traditional materials to keep students engaged
description: The article recommends a balanced approach to remote learning in which schoolchildren intermingle work on electronic devices and work with traditional materials, which the authors suggest "might be optimal". constraints: The authors caution about extrapolating from the limited technology substitution shown in their experiments to full-scale substitution during the pandemic; the balanced approach is offered as an example lesson rather than a tested design in the article.

target_learning_goals: maintaining engagement and motivation in academic subject material during remote learning
examples: Schools could mail workbooks to students or recommend that students print out exercises to break up continuous time on devices; activities such as reading books, running at-home experiments, and art projects can break up extensive technology use.

article_title: Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing
citation: Yoshiki Matsumura, Neil W. Roach, James Heron & Makoto Miyazaki. (2024). Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing. npj Science of Learning 9:34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00241-x
title: Bayesian estimation model with scalar variability for coincidence timing
description: The article adopts a Bayesian estimation account in which the brain learns the statistical distribution of target intervals and integrates it with noisy sensory input, with sensory variability scaling with the interval (scalar variability). This yields a nonlinear TR×TS function (Eq. 4) whose curves diverge between priors only when two independent priors are learned. The authors state that "the /C22TR × TS functions exhibit curves with gentler gradients in the longerTS" because bias toward the prior mean strengthens at longer intervals. Preliminary Experiments I and II verified the predictions.
requirements: Prior distributions imposed across task sessions; measurement of response time intervals across many trials to fit the model curves
constraints: Priors were assumed Gaussian in the model although uniform distributions were used experimentally; the model focuses on prior means, leaving acquired variability (σprior) and Weber fraction unspecified by the fitted curves
target_learners: healthy adult participants performing sensorimotor timing tasks
target_learning_goals: learning statistical distributions (priors) of time intervals for sensorimotor prediction
examples: Preliminary Experiment I presented a single wide prior combining the short and long distributions and confirmed the nonlinear model's predictions

article_title: Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning
citation: Brod, G., Holstein, E., Weindorf, L., Colantonio, J., Bonawitz, E. & Theobald, M. (2025). Do it yourself: discerning the effects of self-directed activity on conceptual learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00364-9
title: Bayesian Yoking Procedure: a three-step computational method for personalized yoked control conditions
description: A novel methodological approach in which each yoked participant observes the responses of an "ideal Bayesian learner" personalized to have that participant's individual prior beliefs. It proceeds in three steps: (1) creating profiles of children's prior belief distributions from pretest data using a hypothesis space of four competing theories (size, material, mass, random guessing) and k-means clustering into six profiles, (2) performing trial-by-trial Bayesian posterior updating for each prototypical profile across the 34 learning trials, and (3) assigning new learners to the best-fitting profile via lowest Wasserstein distance, so yoked children see the responses they would most likely have generated themselves.
requirements: Children's prior beliefs must be assessable via a pretest and mappable to a finite hypothesis space of competing theories
The learning task must allow trial-by-trial Bayesian posterior updating from observed data
Bayesian modeling of children's belief revision in the domain must approximate children's actual responses
constraints: Profile binning was necessary for practical reasons, requiring pre-coding of only six experimental conditions rather than individual matching, which could introduce assignment inaccuracies
It is currently unclear how well the procedure generalizes beyond water displacement; the authors name chemistry, mathematics, and medical reasoning as promising candidates
The optimal Bayesian models predict only the most certain responses, while children respond with some uncertainty on close to 10% of trials, possibly following a sampling hypothesis
target_learning_goals: revision of intuitive causal misconceptions through prediction-feedback learning
examples: Children in the yoked condition observed predictions generated from one of six predefined prior-belief profiles matched via Wasserstein distance to their pretest responses, and the yoked responses matched an individualized ideal model 94.6% of the time

citation: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0
title: Balance learners' working memory capacity with task difficulty to unlock retrieval practice benefits
description: The model implies educational practice should match the difficulty of retrieval practice tasks to learners' working memory capacity. The article states that "achieving the right balance between an individual 's WMC and task dif ﬁculty" may be crucial for unlocking the full potential of retrieval practice for diverse students, providing a mechanistic rationale for the desirable difficulty hypothesis.
requirements: Knowledge of learners' working memory capacity and of the working memory demands of the learning materials
constraints: Tasks that significantly challenge an individual's WMC yield difficulty too high to be beneficial; overly easy testing yields limited benefits
target_learners: students varying in working memory capacity, including low-WMC learners and older adults
target_learning_goals: long-term retention through retrieval practice
examples: The optimal level of difficulty is reached when task demands moderately engage the WMC, allowing both retrieval success and additional processing

article_title: A Bayesian perspective on observers’ inference of group norms
citation: Duan, J., Guo, X., Zheng, L. & Yin, J. (2026). A Bayesian perspective on observers' inference of group norms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00405-x
title: Bayesian inference model of group norm inference
description: The article's computational account treats observers as "lay Bayesians" who integrate observed group behavior with prior beliefs to update the probability that a group norm exists. The model derives posterior probabilities from the number or proportion of norm-consistent behaviors and was compared against a frequency-tracking baseline that relies exclusively on the cumulative tally of observed evidence. In all three experiments its outputs positively predicted participants' judgments, and it captured fine-grained variability that the baseline clustered away.
requirements: Requires manipulation of the number or proportion of norm-consistent behaviors and participants' prior and posterior probability judgments about norm existence.
constraints: The study examines injunctive normative constraints in novel group situations; boundary conditions under which observed behaviors are taken as norm evidence could not be determined in the current study.
target_learners: Adult volunteers judging computer-animated group events
target_learning_goals: Inferring latent group norms from observed behavior patterns in novel social situations
examples: Model-derived posteriors predicted judgmental posteriors (β = 0.69 in Experiment 1; β = 0.87 in Experiment 2) in Bayesian hierarchical regressions with random participant effects.

citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Balance the cognitive demands of motor and learning tasks in digital movement-based learning
description: The article concludes that combining whole-body movement with digital instruction requires deliberately balancing the cognitive load of the motor task against the learning task. It states that "Balancing out the cognitive load demands of the motor and learning tasks is important for facilitation of learning outcomes, as too complex motor tasks may impede learning", and cites the proposal that physically demanding or poorly connected actions can impede learning. The null result is interpreted as consistent with the embodied condition introducing additional dual-task demands rather than reducing extraneous load.
requirements: Designers must calibrate movement complexity and temporal/meaningful connection to the learning task; movement should segment transient information without adding dual-task interference
constraints: The study could not verify the mechanism because cognitive load was not measured; null differences should be interpreted cautiously given the single brief session and simple content
target_learners: Young children in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition supported, rather than impeded, by concurrent physical activity
examples: In the study, whole-body movements were intended to act like segmentation of the transient video, but the authors note the dual-task performance may have been too complex, causing interference

article_title: The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions
citation: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w
title: Balanced learning environments that are knowledge-rich, materially and socially engaging
description: The article describes a recurring design pattern in successful pedagogical alternatives: environments that 'powerfully incorporate both these poles in balanced learning environments that are knowledge-rich, materially and socially engaging'. Such environments reconcile accumulated knowledge with children's joy of learning, balancing playful exploratory discovery with the teaching of what is known. The pattern operationalises the Janus-faced view at the level of the whole learning environment rather than a single activity.
requirements: Environments must draw on accumulated cultural and scientific knowledge while also engaging children as active explorers
constraints: The article notes the interplay of exploration and exploitation in learning sciences literature 'has not been suf ﬁciently uncovered'
target_learners: children in preschool and school education
target_learning_goals: both transmission of accumulated knowledge and fostering of exploration, creativity and innovation
examples: Montessori preschools promoting active hands-on learning with select tools and scaffolding, and Tools-of-the-Mind programmes using cultural tools in play-based, teacher-scaffolded activity

article_title: The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age
citation: Alexandra O. Cohen, Kate Nussenbaum, Hayley M. Dorfman, Samuel J. Gershman and Catherine A. Hartley. (2020). The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age. npj Science of Learning 5:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00075-3
title: Bayesian reinforcement learning with hidden-cause discounting of value updates
description: A family of Bayesian reinforcement learning models in which the learning rate is "dynamically modulated by the posterior probability that an outcome was caused by a hidden agent on each trial", so participants "update their value estimates to a lesser extent when they believe a trial 's outcome can be attributed to the agent". Priors on intervention probability are derived from participants' attribution judgments (empirical Bayesian), estimated from experience (adaptive), or allow impossible interventions (noisy). The study used these models, alongside one-, two-, and three-learning-rate models, to test whether causal structure guides learning across age groups.
requirements: Participants must be able to form beliefs about hidden-agent intervention, measured here via trial-wise attribution judgments used to derive model priors.
constraints: In the task, external causes were invisible and ambiguous; participants could not know with certainty whether any specific outcome was agent-caused.
target_learning_goals: value-based decision making and credit assignment in causally complex probabilistic environments
examples: The empirical Bayesian model reduces value updates proportionally to the participant's belief the agent caused an outcome, e.g., a rock outcome in Robber territory is discounted while a gold outcome is not.

citation: Adamson, D., Dyke, G., Jang, H., & Rosé, C. P. (2014). Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0012-6

description: Bazaar is a publicly available, event-driven architecture for designing multi-party collaborative agents that builds upon the earlier Basilica architecture. undergraduate students in collaborative chat environments

eliciting transactive conversational behavior

citation: McLay, K. F., Thomasse, L., & Reyes, V. C., Jr. (2023). Embracing discomfort in active learning and technology-rich higher education settings: sensemaking through reflexive inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10192-6
title: Bakhtinian dialogism, ideological becoming and chronotope as a framework for sensemaking of teaching discomfort
description: The article deploys Bakhtin's concepts of dialogism, 'ideological becoming' and the chronotope as an explanatory framework for teacher educators' sensemaking. Ideological becoming occurs in 'contact zones' where authoritative discourse (assumed true, "passed down through time as traditional knowledge") meets internally persuasive discourse, which is "neither imposed nor fixed but changeable". Chronotopes are "time–space contexts for an individual's developing ideologies", invoked in professional conversations as 'chunks of history'. The authors use this framework to reconceive discomfort and student resistance as a necessary 'worthwhile struggle' rather than failure.
requirements: Professional conversations with colleagues, in a safe collegial environment, to enable dialogic rather than solitary exploration of discomfort
constraints: The framework is applied to teacher educators' sensemaking in a technology-rich active-learning course; the authors note stressors on higher education can constrain such dialogic engagement
target_learning_goals: Professional identity development
Sensemaking of pedagogical discomfort and failure
examples: The three authors' reflexive 'snapshots' of teaching an educational technology course, analysed through ideological becoming and chronotope

description: The commentary's key implication is that educational technology designers and researchers should consider open science and privacy as values needing balance in their work. article_title: Backward design as a mobile application development strategy
citation: Kantorski, B., Sanford-Dolly, C. W., Commisso, D. R., & Pollock, J. A. (2019). Backward design as a mobile application development strategy. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 711–731. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09662-7
title: Wiggins and McTighe's three-stage backward design framework as a guiding strategy for educational app development
description: Backward design is a curriculum design methodology in which learning goals and assessment are established before instruction is planned. McTighe and Wiggins "formalized the backward design process into three consecutive stages": Stage I identify desired results, Stage II determine acceptable evidence, and Stage III plan learning experiences and instruction. The authors applied all three stages to develop the CityHacks app, arguing it ties learning-goal identification, assessment design, and app feature design into one coherent process.
requirements: Learning goals and acceptable evidence of understanding must be established before learning experiences and instruction are planned
constraints: The authors note design should also involve evaluation and other research theories and practices, so backward design alone is beneficial only "to a certain extent"
target_learning_goals: aligning app design with learning goals and assessment
examples: The team used Stage I to derive three essential questions and enduring understandings about sleep, Stage II to build an in-app debate assessment, and Stage III to choose delivery vehicles such as mini-games, video interviews, and infographics

constraints: Assignments are printed out for students because providing each student a device is currently financially not possible, per the ICT supporter

The model specifies that "learning is student centred", "learning occurs in small student groups", tutors act as facilitators or guides, problems form the organizing focus and stimulus for learning, problems develop problem-solving skills, and new information is attained through self-directed learning. citation: Sasan Baleghizadeh and Atieh Masoun. (2013). The Effect of Self-Assessment on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, Volume 31, Issue 1. https://teslcanadajournal.ca
title: Bandura's social-cognitive account of self-efficacy and its four sources, as applied to language learning
description: The article frames self-efficacy with Bandura's social-cognitive theory, defining it as "an individual's judgement of his or her capabilities to complete a task successfully". It lists four primary sources: enactive mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, social persuasion, and physiological and emotional states, with mastery experiences considered the strongest source. The authors use this framework to explain why self-assessment raised self-efficacy: restating what and how well they had learned made students interpret their performance as a mastery experience.
requirements: Learners must make judgements about their own learning outcomes, per the Boud and Falchikov definition the article adopts
constraints: The article presents this framework as background theory attributed to Bandura, not as a framework it tests directly
target_learning_goals: self-efficacy for learning English as a foreign language
examples: The authors interpret their questionnaire's focus on topics learned, vocabulary gained, and weaknesses as building enactive mastery experience, and the instructor's presentation of successful peer performances as vicarious experience

title: Graspable multimedia framework grounded in Baddeley's working memory theories
description: The study's over-arching framework holds that multimedia for young children should engage the primary senses, particularly hands, to stimulate working memory. Baddeley's WM theories "justifies the use of physical artefacts as a good means to realise the engagement of primary senses of the human, particularly hands, that stimulating the WM in multimedia learning." constraints: The framework's predicted WM benefit was not supported by the study's null main effect

article_title: Can Working Memory Strategies Enhance English Vocabulary Learning?
citation: Ibarra Santacruz, D., & Martínez Ortega, D. (2018). Can working memory strategies enhance English vocabulary learning? HOW, 25(2), 29-47. https://doi.org/10.19183/how.25.2.410
title: Baddeley and Hitch's multi-component working memory model
description: The article's theoretical framework is the Baddeley and Hitch (1974) model of working memory, defined as "a system for temporary storage and control of information necessary for a wide range of complex cognitive activities". It originally comprised three components: the phonological loop (a phonological store plus articulatory rehearsal mechanism for speech-based information), the visuospatial sketchpad for visual and spatial material, and the central executive, which focuses, divides and switches attention and links working memory to long-term memory. A fourth component, the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000), was added to combine information from different sources and link it to long-term knowledge.
requirements: The model explains performance on tasks requiring temporary storage and manipulation of information
constraints: The original model was criticized for the lack of evidence explaining the link between long-term knowledge and working memory, prompting the episodic buffer
target_learners: language learners whose vocabulary learning depends on phonological short-term storage
target_learning_goals: second-language vocabulary learning and retention
examples: The article links the phonological loop's storage capacity and rehearsal mechanism to early-stage vocabulary learning, citing Engel de Abreu and Gathercole (2012)

title: Bartle's four player types as a design lens for appealing gamification elements
description: The article adopts Richard Bartle's (1996) taxonomy of game players as an explanatory framework for designing gamification layers that appeal to varied learners. As printed, "there are four main types of game player: competitors, explorers, achievers and socializers". The article argues that elements such as leaderboards and badges must appeal across these types — leaderboards suit competitors and achievers but not explorers or socializers, group or guild participation suits socializers but not competitors, and finding external resources suits explorers and competitors but not achievers or socializers — which makes gamification design for a wide variety of learners difficult and time-consuming.
requirements: Gamification elements applied to a course should appeal to all the different types of game player in order to be useful for a wide variety of learners
constraints: The article states it is not as simple as making students compete against each other and using a leaderboard, and that designing for varied understandings of gaming makes the design process difficult
target_learners: undergraduate students with varied gaming backgrounds and expectations
target_learning_goals: student engagement with gamified course content
examples: ITM 445 activities were explicitly mapped to player types: solo maker activities were designed to appeal to achiever, explorer and competitor types, duels to competitors, and helper points to socializers and explorers

description: A machine-learning student modeling middleware that records "the learning scene itself, the usage of mouse and keyboard, and the period of time that the learning scene is active" as three evidence nodes and processes them with combined predictive and diagnostic reasoning in a Bayesian network. citation: Corsello, M., Sharma, A., & Jerabek, A. (2015). Successful Transition to High School: A Randomized Controlled Trial of the BARR Model with 9th Grade Students. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555578
title: The BARR model: a comprehensive socio-emotional 9th grade transition approach
description: The Building Assets Reducing Risks (BARR) model is a comprehensive approach addressing developmental, academic, and school environment challenges in 9th grade. It "combines teachers' real-time analysis of student data, student asset building, and intensive teacher collaboration to prevent course failure." The article describes it as unique in being a socio-emotional model producing significant academic results.
requirements: Requires teacher blocks/teams with common preparation periods
Requires weekly block meetings and risk review meetings
constraints: Developed and tested in the context of U.S. high school 9th grade transition programs
target_learning_goals: Core course credit accumulation
Standardized mathematics and reading achievement
Successful transition to high school
examples: Implemented at Saint Louis Park High School in Minnesota since 1998, where course failure dropped from 44-47 percent to 28 percent in one year

title: Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy as a framework for designing journaling interventions
description: The article organizes its intervention design around Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy: "performance accomplishments, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and emotional arousal." Reflective journals are cast as tapping these sources: private journals provide a tangible record of performance accomplishments, peer-shared journals supply vicarious experiences, and teacher comments add verbal persuasion. The framework explains why collaborative journals were expected to outperform non-collaborative ones.

constraints: The study addresses general self-efficacy; the authors note that effects on specific (contextual or situational) self-efficacy remain unexamined and call for future research.

examples: NFC journals documented strategies and their efficacy; PFC learners read classmates' accounts of overcoming learning problems.

title: Balance deep and surface learning approaches in medical curricula rather than relying exclusively on one
description: The article argues that curriculum design should acknowledge "that successful learning in medical education requires a balance between deep and surface learning approaches rather than exclusive reliance on one." Deep strategies such as elaboration support clinical reasoning and long-term retention, while surface strategies including memorization remain necessary for foundational content and assessment demands. The study's finding that balancing understanding and memorization was independently associated with excellent performance supports this principle.

constraints: Traditional lecture-based teaching may emphasize passive learning, which the article associates with reduced learning efficiency

The authors map general self-efficacy to the personal factor, e-learning satisfaction to the contextual factor as students' appraisal of the online environment, and perceived academic performance to the outcome.
