article_title: Input structure-driven instability and convergence in large language model clinical reasoning: a formative study using pediatric residency-level MCQs.
citation: Vinson, J., Caronia, C., & Savargaonkar, R. (2026). Input structure–driven instability and convergence in large language model clinical reasoning: a formative study using pediatric residency–level MCQs. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-48326-4
title: Deliver MCQs to LLMs in structured batches of ten to improve reproducibility and reduce cross-model variability
description: This principle recommends administering multiple questions to LLMs sequentially in batches of ten rather than all at once, because the study found batch delivery converged accuracy to 83%–88% with no significant inter-model differences, while simultaneous delivery produced wide dispersion (38%–90%). The batch size of ten was "selected pragmatically to approximate typical USMLE exam pacing (approximately one question per minute) while remaining within context window limits." The article states this "substantially improves LLM response reproducibility and reduces cross-model variability."
requirements: Batch size of ten items, approximating USMLE exam pacing and remaining within model context window limits
constraints: Only a single batch size (ten items) and fixed presentation order were examined; whether smaller or larger batches maintain stability remains unknown
Batch delivery does not eliminate the risk of factual errors; even at 88% accuracy residual errors could have clinical significance
target_learners: medical educators using LLMs as formative learning tools
target_learning_goals: reliable LLM-supported clinical reasoning practice
stable formative assessment
examples: Each model answered the same 77 validated MCQs under all-at-once and batch-of-ten formats, with batch delivery yielding 83%–88% accuracy and a non-significant ANOVA (F(5,456) = 0.294, ρ = 0.916)

title: Institutions should promote balanced digital habits, mental health support, and integrity-centered assessment reform
description: Based on findings that digital behaviors detrimentally affect mental health and ethical conduct, the authors recommend that "findings highlight the need for institutional policies that promote balanced digital habits, mental health support, and integrity-centered assessment reforms in Ghanaian tertiary institutions." article_title: Basic business knowledge scale for secondary education students. Development and validation with Spanish teenagers.
citation: Bernal-Guerrero Antonio; Cárdenas-Gutiérrez Antonio Ramón; Montoro-Fernández Elisabet. (2020). Basic business knowledge scale for secondary education students. Development and validation with Spanish teenagers. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0235681
title: Three-dimension taxonomy of basic business knowledge for compulsory secondary education (KBM, LK, SK)
description: The article proposes that basic business knowledge in adolescence is configured by three first-order dimensions under a second-order factor. Knowledge in Business Management (KBM) covers "the development of productivity, competitiveness and viability of the company"; Legal Knowledge (LK) covers "the legal and administrative aspects associated with the constitution of a company"; and Strategic Knowledge (SK) refers to the business context for establishing competitive advantage in products or services. The taxonomy was derived from a PRISMA-P systematic review of 24 articles plus expert and student interviews, and confirmed by EFA and CFA.
requirements: Derived for the compulsory secondary stage; the authors state it reflects an adaptation to business contents of that educational stage rather than a full representation of business knowledge
constraints: The authors note the absence of other dimensions more suited to higher education, and that the study was centered on a specific age range, type of school and business education program
target_learners: Compulsory Secondary Education students (Middle School and High School)
target_learning_goals: Formation of basic business knowledge as a foundation for entrepreneurial competence and business identity
examples: The dimensions were identified from 24 selected articles coded with a Fleiss Kappa of K = .82, plus 10 expert interviews and 16 student interviews analyzed in NVivo

title: Balanced, consensus-based peer assessment system with fixed team point allocation
description: A novel peer assessment system developed for a team-based public health project, combining open feedback on preparation, contribution, respect for others' ideas and flexibility with balanced peer marking. description: The authors interpret their self-efficacy findings through Bandura's social cognitive theory, "which suggests four ways to enhance self-efficacy that we identify in the BBNSBT": enactive attainment (performing the action during the role-play simulation), vicarious experience (observing the video and other participants' role-plays), verbal persuasion (facilitator support during debriefings), and psychological safety during the simulations. article_title: Implementation fidelity of a self-management course for epilepsy: method and assessment.
citation: Wojewodka G, Hurley S, Taylor SJC, Noble AJ, Ridsdale L, Goldstein LH. (2017). Implementation fidelity of a self-management course for epilepsy: method and assessment. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-017-0373-x
title: Balance adherence and competence: deliver core content while keeping sessions interactive
description: The article argues that adherence (rigidity) and competence (flexibility) "should be balanced to consistently deliver a complex intervention suitable for a specific context". Facilitators may deliver content as prescribed yet poorly timed or badly communicated, and low competence may affect intervention receipt and enactment of skills. The SMILE(UK) evaluation showed courses could maintain "high levels of adherence to core items while maintaining group interactivity".
requirements: Facilitator training that stresses interactivity and permits adaptation to group needs, alongside checklists of core items
constraints: Increasing adherence may decrease competence, while too much flexibility may undermine delivery of core components
target_learners: adults with poorly controlled epilepsy attending self-management courses
target_learning_goals: behaviour change through self-management education
examples: SMILE(UK) facilitators were encouraged to adapt material to match group needs while core items were measured for adherence

article_title: Basic practical skills teaching and learning in undergraduate medical education - a review on methodological evidence.
citation: Vogel Daniela, Harendza Sigrid. (2016). Basic practical skills teaching and learning in undergraduate medical education – a review on methodological evidence. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5003143/
title: Definition of basic practical skills in undergraduate medical education as physical examination, routine practice-improving, and nurse-performed skills
description: The review defines basic practical skills using three criteria derived from the GMA Committee on Practical Skills consensus statement on 289 practical skills, excluding communication, emergency, and soft skills. A skill qualifies when it matches one of: "physical examination skills which every student should be able to perform independently of the intended postgraduate training", "simple routine medical skills which get better with practice", or "practical skills, which are also performed by nurses". This definition addresses the lack of a unanimous term in the medical education literature.
requirements: Skills must match at least one of the three defining criteria
Exclusion of communication, emergency, and soft skills
constraints: No unanimous term is used in medical education literature to describe basic practical skills
Neither is there a unique definition of which skills can be summarized under basic practical skills
target_learning_goals: Basic practical skills acquisition before clerkships, final year training, or internship
examples: Cardiac auscultation as an example of physical examination skills, venipuncture as a routine skill improving with practice, and bladder catheterization as a skill also performed by nurses.

citation: Multi-society consensus contributors, AANS/CNS, ASNR, AAFITN, CCINR, CING, ESNR, ESMINT, JSNET, SILAN, SNIS, SVIN, WFITN. (2016). title: Baseline qualification pathway: accredited residency plus dedicated neurointerventional fellowship of at least one year at a high-volume center
description: This element is the consensus baseline training pathway for physicians providing intra-arterial acute stroke treatment. It combines residency training with board eligibility or certification and dedicated interventional neuroradiology training under a neurointerventionalist at a high-volume center; the document states "It is preferred that this is a dedicated time (minimum of one year), which occurs after graduating from residency (i.e., a fellowship)." Physicians lacking adequate residency training must spend at least one additional year in clinical neurosciences and neuroimaging before fellowship. Fellowship training must include stroke-specific skills such as microcatheter navigation and complication avoidance and management.
requirements: Dedicated training under the direction of a neurointerventionalist at a high-volume center
Physicians without adequate residency training must spend at least one additional year training in clinical neurosciences and neuroimaging before fellowship
constraints: National accreditation of the training program is strongly preferred but not required; national standards differ in procedure requirements
target_learners: residents and physicians in radiology, neurology or neurosurgery pursuing neuroendovascular training
target_learning_goals: obtaining access in challenging anatomy
microcatheter navigation in the cerebral circulation
use of stroke-specific devices
complication avoidance and management
examples: The guidelines encourage practitioners to meet their national minimum procedural and training standards and note minimum training numbers for stroke thrombectomy may increase in future revisions
